  "title": "STAG: Graph-Topology Guided Rollout Allocation for Agentic RL with Adaptive Signal Fusion",
  "core_problem": "All existing rollout allocation methods for long-horizon agentic RL rely exclusively on model-dependent signals: policy entropy (ARPO), learned exploration tags (Spark), UUCB bounds (InfoTree), static reference-policy variance (PivotRL), or capability-oriented value functions (CoBA-RL). These signals are unreliable early in training when the policy is random, and they cannot capture structural complexity of the environment that is independent of the current policy. Meanwhile, graph-topology signals derived from environment state-transition graphs have been proven valuable for credit assignment (GEPO uses betweenness centrality for advantage estimation; RewardFlow uses graph propagation for reward shaping), but no work has used graph topology for the orthogonal problem of rollout allocation — deciding which prompts deserve more rollouts and which states deserve amplified learning signal. This is a missed opportunity: graph topology encodes environment-structural information about decision complexity that is available from the first training iteration, exactly when model-dependent allocation signals are least reliable.",
  "opportunity": "The rollout allocation landscape has diversified rapidly along the signal axis, but all methods share a blind spot: they ignore environment structure. ARPO (ICLR 2026) uses token-level entropy for adaptive branching. Spark (January 2026) uses SFT-bootstrapped <explore> tags. InfoTree (May 2026) formalizes allocation via UUCB. PivotRL (March 2026) profiles outcome variance from a frozen reference. CoBA-RL (February 2026) allocates via capability-oriented value functions. GRESO (NeurIPS 2025) and PODS (TMLR 2026) filter at the prompt level using reward variance. All are model-dependent. Separately, graph-based methods have demonstrated that environment state graphs encode decision-relevant structure: GEPO (October 2025) constructs state-transition graphs and uses betweenness centrality for credit assignment, achieving +4.1% on ALFWorld and +5.3% on WebShop over GiGPO. RewardFlow (March 2026) uses graph propagation for reward shaping. SALT (EACL 2026) builds trajectory graphs for step-level advantage. But none of these graph-based methods use topology for allocation. The opportunity is clear: graph topology provides a model-free structural signal that is (1) available from training iteration 1, (2) captures environment decision complexity independent of policy state, and (3) is complementary to model-dependent signals that capture epistemic uncertainty. Using graph topology for allocation — not just credit assignment — is a natural extension that no prior work has explored.",
  "landscape": "Credit assignment and rollout efficiency for agentic RL now spans 50+ methods, which we organize by function: (A) Model-dependent rollout allocation: ARPO (ICLR 2026) — entropy-based adaptive branching at tool-call steps. Spark (January 2026) — SFT-bootstrapped <explore> tags for policy-aware branching. InfoTree (May 2026) — UUCB-based submodular allocation with (1-1/e) guarantee. PivotRL (March 2026) — static offline reference-policy variance profiling. CoBA-RL (February 2026) — capability-oriented value function for budget allocation. (B) Prompt/prefix-level allocation: GRESO (NeurIPS 2025) — reward-variance-based prompt filtering. PODS (TMLR 2026) — max-variance rollout down-sampling. Tree-GRPO (ICLR 2026) and Tree Training (November 2025) — prefix computation reuse. PRAISE (April 2026) — prefix reuse for search training. (C) Graph-based credit assignment (NOT allocation): GEPO (October 2025) — constructs state-transition graphs using Sentence-BERT embeddings, uses betweenness centrality for intrinsic rewards, graph-enhanced advantage, and dynamic discount factors; achieves 94.9% on ALFWorld and 80.5% on WebShop with Qwen2.5-7B. RewardFlow (March 2026) — BFS/PPR reward propagation on state graphs. SALT (EACL 2026) — trajectory graphs for step-level advantage. RTMC (April 2026) — rollout tree structure for unbiased per-step MC advantages. (D) Information-gain methods: SIGHT (February 2026) — information-gain scoring for pivotal state identification in search agents with dynamic branching. A2TGPO (May 2026) — information gain with turn-group normalization and adaptive turn-level clipping for credit assignment. (E) Milestone/hierarchical methods: HiPER (February 2026) — 97.4% on ALFWorld via hierarchical plan-execute with HAE. BEACON (May 2026) — milestone-guided dual-scale advantage, 92.9% on ALFWorld. HGPO (ICLR 2026) — hierarchical context-consistent groups. The critical gap: graph-based methods (group C) have proven that state-graph topology encodes valuable decision-relevant structure, but they use this structure exclusively for credit assignment. All rollout allocation methods (groups A, B) use model-dependent or reward-dependent signals. No work uses graph topology for allocation. STAG fills this gap by using graph-topology signals for rollout allocation, providing a model-free structural signal that complements existing model-dependent approaches.",
  "approach": "We propose STAG (State-Topology Augmented Generation), a method that uses environment state-graph topology for rollout allocation in agentic RL. Unlike prior graph-based methods (GEPO, RewardFlow, SALT) that use graphs for credit assignment, STAG uses graphs for allocation — deciding where to focus compute. Unlike prior allocation methods (ARPO, Spark, InfoTree, PivotRL) that rely on model-dependent signals, STAG leverages model-free structural signals from graph topology with adaptive fusion that accounts for their complementary strengths. STAG has four components: (I) Online State-Graph Construction. During standard GRPO training, we construct and incrementally update a state-transition DAG from environment observations. State nodes are defined via domain-specific hash functions on structured environment feedback: ALFWorld uses (location, sorted-inventory, task-progress-flags) tuples from PDDL state; WebShop uses (page-type, search-query-hash, sorted-cart-items, current-product-id) tuples from page observations. Edges represent actions. The graph grows online — new states and transitions from each batch of rollouts expand the existing graph. No learned models (cf. GEPO's Sentence-BERT) or external tools are required. (II) Graph-Topology Allocation Score (GTAS). For each state node v, we compute three topology metrics: (a) Downstream return variance σ²(v) — variance of terminal rewards across rollouts passing through v, capturing decision criticality. (b) Successor diversity H_succ(v) — Shannon entropy over out-edges, measuring action branching. (c) Success path fraction SPF(v) — fraction of successful trajectories passing through v (distinct from standard betweenness centrality; measures success-path coverage rather than shortest-path intermediacy). These are normalized within each batch and combined: I_topo(v) = σ²_norm(v) + H_succ_norm(v) + SPF_norm(v). For each prompt p, the prompt-level allocation score combines graph complexity with reward variance: S(p) = I_prompt(p) × σ²_reward(p), where I_prompt(p) = mean(I_topo(v) for v in G_p). This joint score allocates more rollouts to prompts that are both structurally complex (high graph informativeness) AND have high outcome variance (the model hasn't converged). Rollouts are allocated proportional to S(p) with a floor of n_min to prevent starvation. (III) Topology-Weighted Advantage (TWA). We amplify gradient signal at graph-identified critical states via clipped, normalized reweighting: Ĩ_topo(v) = (I_topo(v) - μ_batch) / σ_batch (batch-normalized), w_topo(v) = clip(1 + α_t · Ĩ_topo(v), 1-ε, 1+ε) with ε = 0.2, A_twa(s,a) = w_topo(s) · A(s,a). The clipping at ±20% prevents gradient amplification at high-variance states where I_topo may correlate with advantage magnitude. This is distinct from GEPO's multi-level advantage interpolation: STAG's reweighting is a lightweight allocation-focused mechanism, not a full credit-assignment redesign. (IV) Phase-Adaptive Signal Scheduling. The weight α_t decreases over training via: α_t = α_0 · (1 - t/T)^β, with α_0 = 0.3, β = 1.5. Motivation: early in training, the policy is near-random and model-dependent signals (entropy, advantage variance) are noisy — graph-topology signals, which capture environment structure independent of policy quality, are more reliable. As training progresses, the policy converges and its signals become informative — graph-topology signals add less marginal value. This directly addresses the limitation that model-free graph signals cannot capture epistemic uncertainty (e.g., a state where the agent consistently takes one action but is stuck in a local optimum would show low graph entropy but high policy confusion). The adaptive schedule ensures STAG gracefully transitions from structure-guided to policy-guided allocation. Key design choices and differentiation: (a) vs. GEPO — GEPO uses graph topology for credit assignment (intrinsic rewards, advantage estimation, dynamic discounting); STAG uses it for allocation (which rollouts to generate, where to focus compute). These are orthogonal and combinable. (b) vs. RewardFlow — RewardFlow uses graph for reward propagation; STAG uses it for allocation. Complementary and combinable. (c) vs. ARPO/Spark/InfoTree — model-free graph topology vs. model-dependent signals; STAG's adaptive scheduling explicitly manages the tradeoff. (d) vs. GRESO/PODS/CoBA-RL — STAG's joint allocation score S(p) = I_prompt × σ²_reward extends reward-variance filtering with structural complexity; STAG also provides state-level signal via TWA, which prompt-level methods cannot. (e) vs. SIGHT/A2TGPO — SIGHT uses information gain for pivotal state identification in search agents; A2TGPO uses IG with turn-group normalization for credit assignment. STAG uses environment-structural signals rather than information-theoretic ones, and targets allocation rather than credit assignment. Failure mode analysis (supporting the method design): We explicitly characterize when graph topology fails vs. when policy signals fail, framing this as motivation for the hybrid design. (a) Graph-topology blind spots: states with low graph entropy (agent consistently takes one action) but high policy confusion (stuck in local optimum). These are missed by STAG but caught by ARPO/Spark. The adaptive schedule mitigates this by reducing graph weight as training reveals these cases. (b) Policy-signal blind spots: states with high structural complexity (many possible paths) but low policy entropy (agent has collapsed to a suboptimal deterministic policy). These are missed by ARPO/Spark but caught by STAG's successor diversity metric. This analysis provides actionable insights for when to use graph vs. policy signals, motivating the adaptive fusion design. Implementation: STAG is implemented as a plugin to verl-agent, adding graph construction hooks to the standard rollout pipeline and modifying the advantage computation. Graph construction is O(rollouts × steps) with hash-based node lookup, adding <5% wall-clock overhead. No changes to the environment interface or rollout generation loop are needed. Evaluation: ALFWorld and WebShop using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct (primary) with verl-agent. Baselines: GRPO (uniform allocation), GRPO+GRESO (prompt-level reward-variance filtering). Reference comparisons: published GEPO, GiGPO, HiPER numbers on the same benchmarks. Primary metrics: (i) success rate at matched compute budget (210 H100-hours total), (ii) training iterations to fixed performance threshold. Method-supporting analysis: (iii) Spearman ρ between GTAS and policy-signal state rankings across training (measuring complementarity), (iv) complementarity ratio — fraction of top-k states identified by only one signal type, (v) failure mode categorization — states classified by graph-topology vs. policy-signal disagreement, (vi) training dynamics of α_t — validating the adaptive schedule by showing complementarity decreases over training. Ablations: (a) prompt-level allocation only vs. TWA only vs. full STAG; (b) individual topology metrics (σ² only vs. H_succ only vs. SPF only vs. combined I_topo); (c) fixed α vs. adaptive α_t schedule; (d) joint allocation score S(p) = I_prompt × σ²_reward vs. I_prompt alone vs. σ²_reward alone (i.e., GRESO). Limitations: (1) Evaluated on structured environments (ALFWorld's PDDL state, WebShop's page structure) where state hashing is well-defined. In truly unstructured environments (WebArena, SWE-bench, Mind2Web), meaningful state graphs may be harder to construct — this is an inherent scope condition for graph-topology methods, not a limitation specific to STAG. (2) 1.5B model scale — though GEPO has shown graph-topology benefits at both 1.5B and 7B scales, validating STAG at 7B is left for future work. (3) The adaptive schedule α_t is a fixed decay; a learned schedule (e.g., bandit-based signal selection) could be more responsive but adds complexity.",

## Reviewer feedback (round 4)
Issues: ["MAJOR: Missing VIP (ICLR 2026, arXiv 2602.01601) — 'Adaptive Rollout Allocation for Online Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards.' VIP is the most directly relevant published work: it solves the same problem (adaptive rollout allocation for GRPO) using a Gaussian process to predict per-prompt success probabilities, accepted at ICLR 2026. While VIP evaluates on math/tool-augmented reasoning (not agent benchmarks), it is the conceptual nearest neighbor for STAG's allocation mechanism and must be cited and differentiated. The differentiation is clear (VIP uses model-dependent predicted success probabilities; STAG uses model-free graph topology) but it must be stated explicitly.", "MAJOR: Missing AERO (arXiv 2602.14338, February 2026) — 'Train Less, Learn More: Adaptive Efficient Rollout Optimization for Group-Based RL.' Uses Bayesian posterior to identify zero-advantage prompts and selective rejection for 48% compute reduction. Another model-dependent allocation method that should appear in the Group A landscape alongside CoBA-RL, GRESO, and PODS.", "MAJOR: Compute budget exceeds the user's hard constraint of ≤200 H100-hours. The stated total is ~210h, already 5% over. Worse, the ablation budget is severely underestimated: the paper proposes 4 ablation categories (allocation vs TWA, individual metrics, fixed vs adaptive α, joint vs single-signal score) totaling 12+ experimental conditions, but only budgets 1 ablation run (~20 GPU-hours). A realistic budget for all proposed experiments is ~300 GPU-hours. Must either: (a) reduce ablation scope to 2-3 key ablations fitting within 200h, or (b) reduce seed count (1 seed for baselines instead of 2) to free budget.", "MINOR: StraTA (arXiv 2605.06642, May 2026) achieves 93.1% on ALFWorld and 84.2% on WebShop via trajectory-level strategy abstraction. While not directly competing (different mechanism), it's a very recent concurrent result on the same benchmarks that should be acknowledged as a reference comparison point.", "MINOR: The joint allocation score S(p) = I_prompt(p) × σ²_reward(p) is a multiplicative combination without theoretical justification. If I_prompt ≈ 0 for structurally simple prompts but σ²_reward is high (the model is confused on a simple task), the score underweights these prompts. Consider whether additive combination S(p) = w₁·I_prompt + w₂·σ²_reward with the adaptive schedule on w₁ would be more robust, or at minimum include the additive variant as an ablation.", "MINOR: The compute budget math is internally inconsistent. GiGPO reports ~363s/iteration for 1.5B on 2×H100, making 150 iterations ≈ 15.1h wall-clock ≈ 30.2 GPU-hours per ALFWorld run. The paper's '~20h per ALFWorld run' appears to underestimate by ~50% if interpreted as GPU-hours, or the total of 210h is inconsistent with 40 GPU-hours per run if '20h' means wall-clock. Clarify the unit and recalculate."]
Feedback: This revision has made substantial progress from Round 3 — the method-first framing, adaptive scheduling, failure mode analysis, and TWA clipping all address prior concerns effectively. The gap is genuinely novel (I independently verified no prior work uses graph topology for allocation). Three changes are needed for a pass:

1. **Cite VIP and AERO immediately**: Add VIP (ICLR 2026) and AERO to the Group A landscape. The differentiation writes itself: VIP/AERO use model-dependent signals (predicted success probability, Bayesian posterior); STAG uses model-free graph topology. STAG's advantage is cold-start reliability (iteration 1); VIP/AERO's advantage is capturing epistemic uncertainty. The adaptive schedule bridges both. This actually STRENGTHENS STAG's narrative — it's the first model-free allocation method in a field of exclusively model-dependent ones.

2. **Fix compute budget to fit ≤200 H100-hours**: Option A: reduce baselines to 1 seed each (saves ~60 GPU-hours), run STAG with 2 seeds for significance testing, and limit ablations to the 2 most important (e.g., allocation-only vs full STAG, and joint vs single-signal — these together tell the strongest story). Option B: run all ablations with fewer training iterations (e.g., 100 instead of 150) and report learning curves. Show the budget math explicitly: list each run, its GPU-hours, and the running total.

3. **Acknowledge StraTA as a reference point**: 93.1% ALFWorld is a strong concurrent result. Frame it as orthogonal (strategy abstraction ≠ rollout allocation) and note combinability.

The paper targets the right venue (EMNLP Findings rather than main track given the scope). The 14-day timeline is tight but feasible if VIP/AERO citations are added quickly and the compute budget is rebalanced. The core insight — that graph topology provides complementary model-free signal for allocation — is sound and well-supported by the failure mode analysis.

## Instructions
- Think in two phases: FIRST reconsider the problem framing (core_problem / opportunity / landscape) if the reviewer flagged issues there, THEN revise the method (approach / resource_estimate / key_references). Do not jump straight to fixing the method if the underlying problem framing needs correction.
- Address each issue specifically.

## 深度调研要求（每一轮修订都必须执行）

不要简单地'打补丁'——每一轮修订都是重新审视和深化这个 idea 的机会。

1. **深度搜索**：针对 reviewer 指出的每个问题，建议用 2-3 种不同的搜索查询调研。
   - 搜索最新的相关论文（arXiv, conference proceedings）
   - 搜索 benchmark/leaderboard 确认当前 SOTA
   - 搜索可能遗漏的相关工作和 concurrent work

2. **深度阅读**：用 WebFetch 实际阅读找到的关键论文的 abstract 和方法部分，
   不要只依赖搜索摘要。形成你自己对领域现状的独立判断。

3. **深度思考**：在修订之前，先独立思考以下问题：
   - 这个 idea 的核心假设是否仍然成立？
   - reviewer 的批评是否揭示了更深层的问题？
   - 有没有更好的 framing 或 approach 来解决同一个核心问题？
   - 修订后的 idea 相比上一版有什么本质性的改进？

4. **避免表面修订**：如果你发现自己只是在换措辞或补充细节而没有实质改进，
   考虑是否需要 major revision 或 pivot。反复的 minor fix 不会拯救一个根基有问题的 idea。

(a) Graph-topology blind spots: states with low graph entropy (agent consistently takes one action) but high policy confusion (stuck in local optimum). (b) Policy-signal blind spots: states with high structural complexity (many possible paths) but low policy entropy (agent has collapsed to a suboptimal deterministic policy). These are missed by ARPO/Spark but caught by STAG's successor diversity metric. This analysis provides actionable insights for when to use graph vs. policy signals, motivating the adaptive fusion design. Implementation: STAG is implemented as a plugin to verl-agent, adding graph construction hooks to the standard rollout pipeline and modifying the advantage computation. # Paper Summary: Adaptive Rollout Allocation for Online Reinforcement Learning

## Title
"Adaptive Rollout Allocation for Online Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards"

## Authors
Hieu Trung Nguyen, Bao Nguyen, Wenao Ma, Yuzhi Zhao, Ruifeng She, and Viet Anh Nguyen

## Problem Addressed
The paper tackles sampling inefficiency in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. Existing methods like GRPO use uniform rollout allocation, treating all training prompts as equally valuable, which wastes computational resources and slows training progress.

## Core Method: VIP (Variance-Informed Predictive)
The approach operates through three key steps:

1. **Probability Prediction**: A lightweight Gaussian process model predicts per-prompt success probabilities using recent rollout data
2. **Variance Translation**: These predictions convert into variance estimates for gradient computation
3. **Optimization**: A convex optimization algorithm determines optimal rollout allocations respecting the computational budget constraint

## Key Innovation
Rather than uniform distribution, VIP allocates more rollouts to prompts that will most reduce gradient variance during policy updates, enabling smarter budget usage.

## Results
The paper reports that VIP "consistently improves sampling efficiency and achieves higher performance than uniform or heuristic allocation strategies in multiple benchmarks."

## Acceptance
Accepted at ICLR 2026

# AERO: Adaptive Efficient Rollout Optimization

## Title
"Train Less, Learn More: Adaptive Efficient Rollout Optimization for Group-Based Reinforcement Learning"

## Authors
Zhi Zhang, Zhen Han, Costas Mavromatis, Qi Zhu, Yunyi Zhang, Sheng Guan, Dingmin Wang, Xiong Zhou, Shuai Wang, Soji Adeshina, Vassilis Ioannidis, and Huzefa Rangwala

## Problem Addressed
AERO tackles a critical inefficiency in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), used for reinforcement learning in large language model alignment. When all rollouts in a generation group produce identical outcomes (all correct or all incorrect), the group-normalized advantages become zero, generating no gradient signal and wasting computational resources.

## Core Mechanisms

**Three key components:**

1. **Adaptive rollout strategy** – Dynamically adjusts generation parameters during training
2. **Selective rejection** – Strategically removes rollouts to maintain useful gradient signals
3. **Bayesian posterior maintenance** – Prevents the model from entering "zero-advantage dead zones" where learning stalls

## Benchmarks
Testing conducted across three Qwen2.5 model configurations:
- Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B
- Qwen2.5-7B
- Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct

Performance measured by Pass@8 and Avg@8 metrics.

## Compute Savings Achieved
- **48% reduction** in total training compute under equivalent rollout budgets
- **45% reduction** in average wall-clock time per training step
- Maintains or improves performance relative to standard GRPO

# StraTA: Strategic Trajectory Abstraction for Agentic RL

## Full Title
"StraTA: Incentivizing Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Strategic Trajectory Abstraction"

## Authors
Xiangyuan Xue, Yifan Zhou, Zidong Wang, Shengji Tang, Philip Torr, Wanli Ouyang, Lei Bai, Zhenfei Yin

## Problem Addressed
The paper tackles a fundamental challenge in optimizing large language models as interactive agents: current approaches rely heavily on reactive methods, which limits both exploration capabilities and credit assignment across lengthy decision sequences.

## Core Method
StraTA introduces a hierarchical framework that samples a high-level strategy from the initial task state, then conditions subsequent actions on that chosen strategy. The approach employs joint training of strategy generation and action execution using a hierarchical GRPO-style rollout design, augmented with diverse strategy sampling and critical self-judgment mechanisms.

## Benchmark Results

**ALFWorld:** Achieved "success rates of 93.1%"

**WebShop:** Attained "84.2%" success rate

**SciWorld:** Reached "63.5% overall score, outperforming frontier closed-source models"

## Key Innovation
The explicit trajectory-level strategy introduces planning foresight into agentic RL, moving beyond purely reactive decision-making to improve both sample efficiency and overall performance across interactive decision-making tasks.

## Overview

AERO (Adaptive Efficient Rollout Optimization) is an enhancement of GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Reinforcement learning plays a central role in large language model post-training, and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is widely used, especially for RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) fine-tuning.

# VIP: Variance-Informed Predictive Allocation - Key Details

## Evaluation Benchmarks

VIP does **not** evaluate on agent benchmarks like ALFWorld or WebShop. Instead, it tests on:

1. **Mathematical reasoning**: DAPO-MATH-17k training set, evaluated on AIME2024 and AIME2025
2. **Tool-augmented reasoning**: MuSiQue (19,938 prompts) for training, tested on Bamboogle and MuSiQue test sets

The experiments use three backbone models: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct.

## Gaussian Process Model Purpose

The GP model predicts per-prompt success probabilities at each training iteration. As stated in the paper, it "predict[s] the success probability of the current model on each training prompt" using prompt embeddings and a radial basis function kernel, enabling recursive Bayesian updates as new rollout data arrives.

## Convex Optimization for Allocation

The optimization minimizes expected gradient variance subject to budget constraints. The paper formulates a continuous relaxation problem with closed-form solutions via bisection search, then applies a greedy rounding heuristic to produce integer allocations respecting per-prompt rollout bounds.

## Key Theoretical Result

The primary theoretical contribution establishes that "the gradient variance contributed by a prompt...depend[s] on the probability that it is solved by the current model." Specifically, Propositions 4.2-4.3 derive exact variance formulas proportional to p(1-p), where p represents success probability.
